relevance_reason: This is a case report of a newborn with the c.4A>G SHOC2 mutation, the variant that causes NSLH1, who had severe hydrops fetalis. It adds hydrops to the clinical spectrum of the disorder.

findings.statement: Gargano et al. (2014) reported severe hydrops fetalis in a preterm newborn heterozygous for the c.4A>G missense change in SHOC2. They concluded that hydrops is a clinically relevant complication of Noonan-like syndrome with loose anagen hair, as it is in other RASopathies such as Noonan, cardiofaciocutaneous, and Costello syndromes.
quotes: Here, we report on the occurrence of severe hydrops in a newborn heterozygous for the invariant c.4A>G missense change in SHOC2 which underlies Noonan-like syndrome with loose anagen hair, documenting that it represents a clinically relevant complication in this condition, shared by RASopathies.

findings.statement: Gargano et al. (2014) found that a preterm newborn with severe hydrops fetalis was heterozygous for the recurrent ('invariant') c.4A>G missense mutation in SHOC2, the change that underlies Noonan-like syndrome with loose anagen hair.
quotes: Hydrops fetalis in a preterm newborn heterozygous for the c.4A>G SHOC2 mutation.

relevance_reason: Reports a patient with molecularly confirmed NSLH (SHOC2 c.4A>G) who developed neuroblastoma, and screens pediatric cancer cohorts for somatic SHOC2 variants.

findings.statement: Garavelli et al. (2015) reported a child with molecularly confirmed Noonan syndrome-like disorder with loose anagen hair (NSLH) who developed a neuroblastoma, first suspected at 3 months of age by abdominal ultrasound examination. The authors noted this was the second instance of neuroblastoma in NSLH and suggested a possible predisposition to this malignancy in individuals heterozygous for the SHOC2 c.4A>G mutation.
quotes: Here, we report on a child with molecularly confirmed NSLH who developed a neuroblastoma, first suspected at the age 3 months by abdominal ultrasound examination.
this second instance of neuroblastoma in NSLAH suggests a possible predisposition to this malignancy in subjects heterozygous for the c.4A>G SHOC2 mutation.

findings.statement: Following this observation, Garavelli et al. (2015) scanned the SHOC2 coding sequence encompassing the c.4A>G change in selected pediatric cohorts of malignancies documented to occur in RASopathies (neuroblastoma, brain tumors, rhabdomyosarcoma, acute lymphoblastic leukemia, and myeloid leukemia) but did not identify a functionally relevant cancer-associated variant, concluding that the results do not support a major role for somatic SHOC2 mutations in these pediatric cancers.
quotes: scanning of the SHOC2 coding sequence encompassing the c.4A>G change was performed on selected pediatric cohorts of malignancies documented to occur in RASopathies (i.e., neuroblastoma, brain tumors, rhabdomyosarcoma, acute lymphoblastic, and myeloid leukemia), but failed to identify a functionally relevant cancer-associated variant.
While these results do not support a major role of somatic SHOC2 mutations in these pediatric cancers

findings.statement: Garavelli et al. (2015) described NSLH (Mazzanti syndrome) as a RASopathy characterized by Noonan syndrome-like craniofacial features, cardiac defects, cognitive deficits and behavioral issues, reduced growth generally associated with GH deficit, darkly pigmented skin, and a unique combination of ectodermal anomalies, virtually always caused by the invariant SHOC2 c.4A>G (p.Ser2Gly) mutation.
quotes: is a RASopathy characterized by craniofacial features resembling Noonan syndrome, cardiac defects, cognitive deficits and behavioral issues, reduced growth generally associated with GH deficit, darkly pigmented skin, and an unique combination of ectodermal anomalies.
Virtually all cases of NSLH are caused by an invariant and functionally unique mutation in SHOC2 (c.4A>G, p.Ser2Gly).

relevance_reason: Paper identifies the recurrent de novo SHOC2 c.4A>G (S2G) mutation as the cause of Noonan-like syndrome with loose anagen hair, gives a clinical description of the patients, and reports functional work and a C. elegans model.

findings.statement: Cordeddu et al. (2009) selected SHOC2 as a candidate gene using an in silico protein-interaction network analysis seeded with known RAS-MAPK disease proteins. In 96 Noonan syndrome patients without mutations in the known genes, they found a heterozygous 4A-G transition in SHOC2, predicting a ser2-to-gly (S2G) substitution, in 4 unrelated sporadic patients. In the 3 patients whose parents were available, the mutation was de novo. It was present in several tissues, which pointed to germline origin.
quotes: Resequencing of coding exons for the best candidate, SHOC2, in a NS cohort including 96 individuals who were negative for mutations in known disease genes
revealed an A-to-G transition at position 4 of the gene, predicting the Ser2Gly amino acid substitution (S2G), in four unrelated individuals
All cases were sporadic, and genotyping of parental DNAs available for three of the four subjects documented the absence of the sequence variant in the parents and confirmed paternity in each family

findings.statement: Cordeddu et al. (2009) then screened 410 mutation-negative patients with Noonan syndrome or a related phenotype. They found the same SHOC2 4A>G (S2G) change in 21 of them and showed it was de novo in the 12 families where parental DNA was available. They found no other disease-associated SHOC2 variant, which they said strongly suggested a specific pathogenic role for S2G. In total, 25 patients carried the mutation.
quotes: We then analyzed SHOC2 in a cohort of 410 mutation-negative subjects with NS or a related phenotype. We observed 21 with the 4A>G missense change and proved that mutations were de novo in twelve families from which parental DNAs were available.
No additional disease-associated SHOC2 sequence variant was identified in the analyzed cohort, strongly suggesting a specific pathogenetic role for the S2G amino acid substitution.

findings.statement: Cordeddu et al. (2009) found that the 25 patients with the SHOC2 mutation shared a consistent phenotype, previously termed Noonan-like syndrome with loose anagen hair. Facial features looked typical of Noonan syndrome. Patients had reduced growth, often with proven growth hormone deficiency, cognitive deficits, and hyperactive behavior that improved with age. Hair was easily pluckable, sparse, thin and slow-growing, and loose anagen hair was confirmed by microscopy in 12. Most patients also had darkly pigmented skin with eczema or ichthyosis. Cardiac anomalies were present in most, with mitral valve dysplasia and septal defects overrepresented. The voice was hypernasal. Several patients had been thought as infants to have features suggestive of Costello or cardiofaciocutaneous syndrome.
quotes: they exhibited reduced growth, which was frequently associated with proven GH deficiency, cognitive deficits, distinctive hyperactive behaviour that improved with age in most subjects, and hair anomalies including easily pluckable, sparse, thin, slow growing hair. In twelve subjects, a diagnosis of loose anagen hair was confirmed by microscopic examination of pulled hairs.

Most of them also exhibited darkly pigmented skin with eczema or ichthyosis. Cardiac anomalies were observed in the majority of the cases, with dysplasia of the mitral valve and septal defects significantly overrepresented compared with the general NS population. The voice was characteristically hypernasal.
Common features include macrocephaly, high forehead, hypertelorism, palpebral ptosis, low-set/posteriorly rotated ears, short and webbed neck, and pectus anomalies.

phenotypes.text: easily pluckable sparse thin slow-growing hair

findings.statement: Cordeddu et al. (2009) showed that the S2G substitution creates an N-myristoylation site in SHOC2. In Cos-1 cells, SHOC2 S2G took up [3H]-myristic acid, but wildtype SHOC2 and the disease-unrelated S2A mutant did not. Wildtype SHOC2 was spread through the cytoplasm and nucleus and moved to the nucleus after EGF stimulation. In contrast, S2G was targeted to the plasma membrane and did not move to the nucleus. An inhibitor of N-myristoyltransferase reduced or abolished the membrane localization of the mutant.
quotes: SHOC2S2G incorporated [3H]-myristic acid, while the wild type protein and the disease-unrelated SHOC2S2A did not.

SHOC2wt was uniformly distributed in the cytoplasm and nucleus in starved cells but was restricted to the nucleus following EGF stimulation, implying an unexpected role for this protein in signal transduction. In contrast, SHOC2S2G was specifically targeted to the cell membrane in both states.

Treatment with 2-hydroxymyristic acid, an NMT inhibitor, at varying doses reduced or abolished SHOC2S2G’s membrane localization (Supplementary Fig. 2 online), confirming a dependency upon myristoylation.

findings.statement: Cordeddu et al. (2009) found that SHOC2 S2G did not form heterodimers with wildtype SHOC2 and did not block the wildtype protein from moving to the nucleus, which ruled out a dominant-negative effect. In Neuro2A neuroblastoma cells, but not in Cos-1 or 293T cells, the mutant increased EGF-dependent ERK phosphorylation compared with wildtype. The authors proposed that constant membrane localization of SHOC2 S2G prolongs PP1C-mediated dephosphorylation of RAF1 at ser259, which would sustain MAPK activation.
quotes: The experiments demonstrated that these proteins do not heterodimerize, ruling out that possibility.

While we did not observe significant change in ERK activation in Cos-1 and 293T cells (data not shown), SHOC2S2G expression promoted enhanced EGF-dependent ERK phosphorylation compared to wild type SHOC2, in neuroblastoma Neuro2A cells (Fig. 3c).

constitutive membrane translocation of the disease-causing SHOC2S2G is expected to promote prolonged PP1C-mediated RAF1 dephosphorylation at Ser259 and, consequently, sustained RAF1-stimulated MAPK activation

findings.statement: Cordeddu et al. (2009) showed in C. elegans that wildtype human SHOC2 could functionally replace sur-8, but SHOC2 S2G could not. When induced in wildtype worms at the early L3 stage, S2G caused protruding vulva, reduced egg laying and a bag-of-worms phenotype. Wildtype SHOC2 with an added N-myristoylation sequence gave the same result, but untagged wildtype SHOC2 did not. These new (neomorphic) defects came from abnormal vulval morphogenesis rather than a change in how vulval cell fate was specified.
quotes: While SHOC2wt was able to replace SUR-8 functionally, SHOC2S2G failed to do so.

at early L3 stage, it caused abnormal vulval development, resulting in protruding vulva (Pvl), decreased egg laying efficiency (Egl) and accumulation of larvae inside the mother with the formation of bag-of-worms adults (Bag phenotype)
These neomorphic phenotypes were absent in animals expressing SHOC2wt but were also observed when SHOC2wt tagged with an N-myristoylation sequence (myr::SHOC2wt) was expressed

relevance_reason: Case report of a molecularly confirmed NS/LAH patient with SHOC2 c.4A>G, describing GH insensitivity and chronic complex tics.

findings.statement: Capalbo et al. (2012) reported a patient with molecularly confirmed Noonan-like syndrome with loose anagen hair (NS/LAH) who had severe short stature associated with growth hormone insensitivity and chronic complex tics. The authors said tics had never been described before in this syndrome. The most common causes of secondary tics in childhood were excluded.
quotes: We report on a patient with molecularly confirmed NS/LAH exhibiting severe short stature associated with GH insensitivity (GHI), and chronic complex tics, a neurological feature never described before in this syndrome.
Most common causes of secondary tics in childhood were excluded.

findings.statement: In the NS/LAH patient reported by Capalbo et al. (2012), an IGF1 generation test showed only a blunted increase in IGF1 after exogenous GH treatment. This indicated mild GH insensitivity, with STAT5 activation that was normal.
quotes: IGF1 generation test revealed only a blunted increase in IGF1 after exogenous GH treatment, revealing mild GH insensitivity associated with proper STAT5 activation.

findings.statement: Capalbo et al. (2012) noted that NS/LAH has been related to the invariant c.4A>G missense change in SHOC2 and has features reminiscent of Noonan syndrome. Common features include ectodermal involvement, short stature with growth hormone deficiency, and cognitive deficits.
quotes: Noonan-like syndrome with loose anagen hair (NS/LAH; OMIM 607721), recently related to the invariant c.4A>G missense change in SHOC2, is characterized by features reminiscent of Noonan syndrome.
Ectodermal involvement, short stature associated with growth hormone (GH) deficiency (GHD), and cognitive deficits are common features.

relevance_reason: Case report of a patient with NSLH1 (SHOC2-related) with cleft palate and hypopituitarism, which expands the phenotype.

findings.statement: Couser et al. (2018) reported a female patient with NSLH1 who was born with a posterior cleft palate, micrognathia, and mild hypotonia. In childhood and young adulthood she developed hearing loss, strabismus, and hypopituitarism with growth hormone, thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), and gonadotropin deficiencies. The authors noted that true cleft palate did not appear to have been reported before in NS or NSLH, and that endocrine abnormalities other than growth hormone deficiency are rarely documented. They suggested that the SHOC2 mutation may be responsible for the cleft palate and hypopituitarism.
quotes: We present a female patient with NSLH1 who was born with a posterior cleft palate, micrognathia, and mild hypotonia.
Other findings in her childhood and young adulthood years include hearing loss, strabismus, and hypopituitarism with growth hormone, thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH), and gonadotropin deficiencies.
The SHOC2 mutation may be responsible for this patient's additional features of cleft palate and hypopituitarism.

findings.statement: Couser et al. (2018) stated that every NSLH1 case reported to date, including their patient, carried the SHOC2 c.4A>G (p.Ser2Gly) mutation.
quotes: All NSLH1 reported cases to date have had an SHOC2 c.4A>G, p.Ser2Gly mutation

findings.statement: Couser et al. (2018) described Noonan-like syndrome with loose anagen hair as having the typical features of Noonan syndrome plus macrocephaly and loose anagen hair. Some patients have growth hormone deficiency, and intellectual disability is more common than in Noonan syndrome.
quotes: Noonan-like syndrome with loose anagen hair (NSLH, including NSLH1, OMIM #607721 and NSLH2, OMIM #617506) is characterized by typical features of NS with additional findings of macrocephaly, loose anagen hair, growth hormone deficiency in some, and a higher incidence of intellectual disability.

relevance_reason: Case report of an NSLH patient with the SHOC2 S2G mutation and moyamoya syndrome, which widens the phenotype to include cerebrovascular anomalies.

findings.statement: Choi et al. (2015) reported a girl diagnosed at age 6 years with Noonan-like syndrome with loose anagen hair, based on profound short stature and ectodermal anomalies including sparse, easily pluckable hair. At age 10 years she had recurrent left hemiplegia from transient ischemic attacks. Cerebrovascular imaging showed occlusion or narrowing of both internal carotid arteries and both middle cerebral arteries, with distal moyamoya-like vessels. The authors stated that this was the first reported case of NSLH with moyamoya syndrome.
quotes: A 6-year-old girl was diagnosed with Noonan-like syndrome with loose anagen hair because of profound short stature and ectodermal anomalies such as sparse and easily pluckable hair.

At age 10, she manifested recurrent left hemiplegia. Moreover, cerebrovascular imaging revealed occlusion or narrowing of both internal carotid arteries and both middle cerebral arteries with distal moyamoya-like vessels.
We describe the first case of Noonan-like syndrome with loose anagen hair associated with moyamoya syndrome

findings.statement: Choi et al. (2015) found a heterozygous c.4A>G (p.S2G) mutation in the SHOC2 gene in a girl with NSLH and moyamoya syndrome.
quotes: A heterozygous mutation of c.4A>G (p.S2G) in the SHOC2 gene was identified

findings.statement: Choi et al. (2015) started recombinant human growth hormone in their patient with NSLH at 8 years of age. After moyamoya syndrome developed, she was treated with aspirin and a calcium channel blocker.
quotes: recombinant human growth hormone therapy was initiated at 8 years of age
She is treated with aspirin and calcium channel blocker.

relevance_reason: The original clinical description that proposed Noonan-like syndrome with loose anagen hair as a new syndrome.

findings.statement: Mazzanti et al. (2003) described 3 children with short stature, the same facial phenotype, macrocephaly, enlarged cerebrospinal fluid spaces, and a short neck with redundant skin. They also had severe growth hormone (GH) deficiency, mild psychomotor delay with attention deficit-hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), and a unique combination of ectodermal abnormalities, including darkly pigmented, hairless skin and hair defined as loose anagen hair. Two of the 3 children had mild dilatation of the pulmonary root.
quotes: We present three children with short stature, the same facial phenotype, macrocephaly, enlarged cerebral spinal fluid spaces, short neck with redundant skin, severe GH deficiency, mild psychomotor delay with attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), mild dilatation of the pulmonary root in two of them, and a unique combination of ectodermal abnormalities.
the behavioral phenotype, GH deficiency, darkly pigmented and hairless skin, and the unusual aspect of the hair, defined as loose anagen hair syndrome did not fit any known condition

phenotypes.text: mild dilatation of the pulmonary root

findings.statement: Mazzanti et al. (2003) noted that the appearance of their 3 patients was not completely typical of Noonan syndrome. Together with the behavioral phenotype, GH deficiency, and ectodermal findings, this did not fit any known condition. They postulated that the patients may represent a distinct, previously unreported syndrome, which they named 'Noonan-like syndrome with loose anagen hair.'
quotes: Their appearance, not completely typical of Noonan syndrome, the behavioral phenotype, GH deficiency, darkly pigmented and hairless skin, and the unusual aspect of the hair, defined as loose anagen hair syndrome did not fit any known condition.
We postulate that these children may represent a distinct, previously unreported syndrome that we would name "Noonan-like syndrome with loose anagen hair".

relevance_reason: This paper reports two more patients with NSLH who carry heterozygous germline SHOC2 mutations and also have moyamoya disease, which adds a cerebrovascular feature to the phenotype.

findings.statement: Lo et al. (2015) described 2 individuals with Noonan-like syndrome with loose anagen hair (NSLH) who also had moyamoya disease, a chronic cerebrovascular condition caused by progressive stenosis of the arteries around the circle of Willis with prominent arterial collateral circulation.
quotes: we describe two individuals with NSLH who also have moyamoya disease and in whom heterozygous germline mutation in SHOC2 was found
Moyamoya disease is a unique chronic cerebrovascular condition caused by progressive stenosis of the arteries around the circle of Willis with prominent arterial collateral circulation.

findings.statement: In 2 individuals with NSLH and moyamoya disease, Lo et al. (2015) identified a heterozygous germline mutation in the SHOC2 gene.
quotes: we describe two individuals with NSLH who also have moyamoya disease and in whom heterozygous germline mutation in SHOC2 was found

relevance_reason: Functional study of SHOC2 domains that control its subcellular shuttling and the plasma-membrane mistargeting of the Mazzanti syndrome-causing p.Ser2Gly mutant, with effects on ERK signalling.

findings.statement: Motta et al. (2016) found that leucine-rich repeats 1 to 13 of SHOC2 form a structurally recognizable domain. This domain was required for SHOC2 import into the nucleus and for the constitutive plasma membrane targeting of the SHOC2 S2G mutant. The N-terminal region rich in KEKE motifs was needed for efficient SHOC2 export from the nucleus.
quotes: We show that LRRs 1 to 13 constitute a structurally recognizable domain required for SHOC2 import into the nucleus and constitutive targeting of SHOC2S2G to the plasma membrane, while the KEKE motif-rich region is necessary to achieve efficient SHOC2 export from the nucleus.

findings.statement: Motta et al. (2016) found that the Mazzanti syndrome-associated SHOC2 S2G mutant localized to both raft and non-raft membrane domains and moved to non-raft domains after stimulation. Trapping SHOC2 at different subcellular sites affected the strength and timing of ERK signalling in different ways. The authors suggested that SHOC2 plays a dual, counteracting role in controlling ERK signalling from different intracellular compartments.
quotes: We also document that SHOC2S2G localizes both in raft and non-raft domains, and that it translocates to the non-raft domains following stimulation.

we demonstrate that SHOC2 trapping at different subcellular sites has a diverse impact on ERK signalling strength and dynamics, suggesting a dual counteracting modulatory role of SHOC2 in the control of ERK signalling exerted at different intracellular compartments.

relevance_reason: Reports 8 patients with the SHOC2 p.S2G mutation and describes their Noonan-like phenotype with loose anagen/easily pluckable hair.

findings.statement: Komatsuzaki et al. (2010) analyzed SHOC2 in 92 patients with Noonan syndrome and related disorders who had no mutations in PTPN11, KRAS, HRAS, BRAF, MAP2K1/2, SOS1, or RAF1, and found the previously identified p.S2G mutation in 8 patients.
quotes: we analyzed SHOC2 in 92 patients with Noonan syndrome and related disorders who did not exhibit PTPN11, KRAS, HRAS, BRAF, MAP2K1/2, SOS1 or RAF1 mutations. We found the previously identified p.S2G mutation in eight of our patients.

findings.statement: Komatsuzaki et al. (2010) reported that all 8 patients with the SHOC2 p.S2G mutation had short stature, sparse hair, and atopic skin; 6 had severe mental retardation and easily pluckable hair, and 1 had leukocytosis. The authors concluded that clinical manifestations partially overlap with typical Noonan or CFC syndrome and that easily pluckable/loose anagen hair is distinctive in SHOC2 mutation-positive patients.
quotes: All the patients with the p.S2G mutation showed short stature, sparse hair and atopic skin. Six of the mutation-positive patients showed severe mental retardation and easily pluckable hair, and one showed leukocytosis.
show that easily pluckable/loose anagen hair is distinctive in SHOC2 mutation-positive patients

findings.statement: Komatsuzaki et al. (2010) developed a rapid detection system for the SHOC2 p.S2G mutation using melting curve analysis, useful for screening for this apparently common mutation.
quotes: We developed a rapid detection system to identify the p.S2G mutation using melting curve analysis, which will be a useful tool to screen for the apparently common mutation.

findings.statement: Komatsuzaki et al. (2010) identified no SHOC2 mutations in leukemia cells from 82 leukemia patients.
quotes: No SHOC2 mutations were identified in leukemia cells from 82 leukemia patients.

relevance_reason: Case report of a patient with NSLH1 caused by a de novo SHOC2 p.S2G variant who developed systemic lupus erythematosus.

findings.statement: Uehara et al. (2018) reported a 28-year-old man with Noonan syndrome-like disorder with loose anagen hair who had intellectual disability, short stature, dysmorphic facial features, and thin hair. He developed hypertrophic cardiomyopathy at age 7 years and afebrile generalized seizures at age 18 years. At age 24 years, he presented with 3 days of intermittent fever, right chest pain, and a malar butterfly rash; he fulfilled both the ACR and SLICC criteria for systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).
quotes: The proband was a 28-year-old male patient with intellectual disabilities, a short stature, dysmorphic facial features, and thin hair. He developed hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and afebrile generalized seizures at the ages of 7 and 18 years, respectively.

At the age of 24 years, he presented with a 3-day history of intermittent fever accompanied by right chest pain and a malar butterfly rash. He fulfilled both the American College of Rheumatology (ACR) criteria and the Systemic Lupus International Collaborating Clinics (SLICC) criteria for SLE

findings.statement: In a man with NSLH1 and SLE, Uehara et al. (2018) identified a de novo SHOC2 variant (c.4A>G, p.S2G) by medical exome sequencing.
quotes: Medical exome sequencing identified a de novo SHOC2 variant (c.4A > G, p.S2G).

findings.statement: The SLE in the patient with NSLH1 reported by Uehara et al. (2018) was successfully treated with prednisolone.
quotes: was successfully treated with prednisolone

findings.statement: Uehara et al. (2018) noted that SLE had been reported in 5 patients with RASopathies (3 with SHOC2 variants, 1 with PTPN11, 1 with KRAS) and suggested that the association between SHOC2 variants and SLE represents more than a chance association; they recommended that SLE be suspected in patients with constitutional SHOC2 pathogenic variants who have fever of unknown origin.
quotes: Five patients have been reported: three with SHOC2 variants, one with a PTPN11 variant, and one with a KRAS variant.
We suggest that the association between SHOC2 variant and SLE represents more than a chance association.
In the event of fever of unknown origin in patients with constitutional SHOC2 pathogenic variant, SLE should be suspected.

relevance_reason: The paper describes two further patients with NS/LAH who carry the SHOC2 c.4A>G (p.Ser2Gly) mutation. It reports how their features differ and the different growth hormone axis defects behind their short stature.

findings.statement: Capalbo et al. (2012) described a girl (patient 1) born at 34 weeks to nonconsanguineous parents after a pregnancy complicated by polyhydramnios. She was referred at age 7 years for severe short stature (height -5.7 SDS) and had a bone age delayed by 3 years. She had macrocephaly, high forehead, epicanthic folds, palpebral ptosis, hypertelorism, a high narrow palate, pterygium colli, pectus excavatum with widely spaced nipples, deep palmar and plantar creases, mild psychomotor delay (IQ 52) and a hypoplastic corpus callosum. Over time she developed ectodermal abnormalities (nail dystrophy, sparse and easily pulled hair, and dark hairless skin). At 9 years she developed complex motor and vocal tics, then a generalized seizure; MRI also showed a diffuse reduction in white matter.
quotes: Physical examination revealed macrocephaly, high forehead, epicanthic folds, palpebral ptosis, hyperthelorism, high and narrow palate, pterigium colli, pectus excavatum with widely spaced nipples, deep palmar and plantar creases (Figure 1a).

Over time, several ectodermal abnormalities became evident, including nail dystrophy, dry, fine textured, sparse hair, which were easily pulled from the scalp, and dry, hairless, darkly pigmented skin.

At 9 years, she suddenly presented with complex motor and vocal tics characterized by repetitive stereotyped movements predominantly involving facial and shoulder muscles and repetitive sounds, which persisted for more than 1 year.

findings.statement: Capalbo et al. (2012) described a second girl (patient 2), born at term to nonconsanguineous parents with a head circumference above the 90th centile and a large atrial septal defect. She was referred at age 9 years for short stature (height -3.21 SDS) and had a bone age delayed by 2 years. She had macrocephaly, high forehead, epicanthic folds, a low-set ear, hypertelorism, short neck with redundant skin, pectus excavatum, fine sparse hair, darkly pigmented skin with cafe-au-lait spots, hyperextensible joints, mild scoliosis, mild psychomotor delay (IQ 65) with behavioral problems that later improved, and Chiari type I malformation. Puberty was delayed, and she started hormone replacement at age 16.
quotes: At birth, a large atrial septal defect with pulmonary hyperflow was detected.

Physical examination revealed macrocephaly, high forehead, epicanthic folds, low-set and posterior angulated left ear, hyperthelorism, short neck with redundant skin, pectus excavatum, fine, dry, fine textured, sparse hair, darkly pigmented skin with cafe au lait spots, tuberous angioma in the left hypochondrium, hyperextensible joints and mild scoliosis (Figure 1b).
She had only a mild psychomotor delay (IQ 65) and behavioral problems. Cerebral MRI showed type I Chiari malformation.

findings.statement: Capalbo et al. (2012) found the SHOC2 c.4A>G (p.Ser2Gly) mutation in both patients, confirming the diagnosis of NS/LAH. Patient 1 had first been screened for mutations in PTPN11, KRAS, SOS1, MEK1 and BRAF, and none were found.
quotes: Such a distinctive association prompted SHOC2 mutation analysis which confirmed the presence of the disease-causing mutation (c.4A > G, p.Ser2Gly), thus confirming diagnosis of NS/LAH.
The complex clinical phenotype prompted to the clinical diagnosis of NS/LAH and molecular analysis of SHOC2 revealed the presence of the disease-causing mutation (c.4A > G, p.Ser2Gly).
Based on these features, NS disease genes were screened (PTPN11, KRAS, SOS1, MEK1, BRAF) but mutation analysis failed to reveal any causative mutation.

findings.statement: Capalbo et al. (2012) found that patient 1 had low serum IGF1, a normal GH peak after arginine stimulation, and only a mild IGF1 rise on an IGF1 generation test, which they interpreted as GH insensitivity. Her GHR gene was normal, and GH-induced tyrosine phosphorylation of STAT5 was normal. Patient 2 had a low GH peak after clonidine and arginine stimulation, with IGF1 at the lower limit of normal, which indicated partial GH deficiency. The authors noted that GH insensitivity had not previously been described in NS/LAH.
quotes: revealed low serum levels of IGF1 (27 ng/ml, nv 60–350) and normal GH peak after arginine stimulation (16 ng/ml), thus excluding a GHD and suggesting a condition of mild GH insensitivity (GHI).
GHI was not related to mutations in GH receptor in that molecular analysis of GHR gene was normal.

revealed abnormal GH peak after clonidine stimulation (9 ng/ml) and arginine stimulation (5.3 ng/dL) with serum levels of IGF1 at the lower limit of normal range (70.4 ng/ml), indicative of a condition of partial GH deficiency

findings.statement: Capalbo et al. (2012) reported that recombinant human GH therapy did not significantly improve linear growth in patient 1, who had GH insensitivity. Her growth velocity stopped when treatment was withdrawn, and after 6 years of treatment her height remained -5 SDS. Patient 2, who had partial GH deficiency, showed only a blunted response to GH therapy.
quotes: The patient underwent a therapeutic trial with recombinant human (rh) GH at a mean dose of 45 μg/kg/die. However, no significant improvement in linear growth was observed.
Despite a 6-years GH treatment, she still has a severe short stature (height −5 SDS) (Figure 2a), and IGF1 levels well below the normal range (93.5 ng/ml; nv 180–780).
She was then started on recombinant human (rh) GH at a mean dose of 40 μg/kg/die, with only a blunted response to treatment (Figure 2b).

findings.statement: Capalbo et al. (2012) noted that their 2 patients with the same SHOC2 mutation had different phenotypes. Patient 1 had more pronounced features, epilepsy, and chronic tics, which had not previously been reported with SHOC2 mutations, while patient 2's mild delay improved over time. The authors suggested that the SHOC2 mutation may alter GHR signaling through RAS-MAPK dysregulation. They also speculated that modifier genes and environmental factors could explain the clinical heterogeneity.
quotes: Patient 1 also had epilepsy and atypical neurologic signs such as chronic vocal and motor tics, never previously reported in patients with SHOC2 mutations or in any other condition due to RAS-MAPK dysregulation.
However, it is conceivable that SHOC2 mutation alters GHR signaling through dysregulation of RAS-MAPK pathway, thus contributing to cause GHI.
Disease modifying genes, variation in environmental exposures, as well as system dynamics may come into play in modulating clinical expression of the disease.
